strengths: The proposed method is well motivated: unlike FisherRF-style parameter-variance approaches, the paper builds explicit Gaussian primitive representations of training-view visibility and reconstruction error (Eqs. 3–8), which are intuitive, cheap to compute, and applicable purely as post-processing without interfering with GS training.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this topic: two datasets (LF and TUM), two error targets (depth and rendering), single-view vs. multi-view and multi-scene regression training regimes, in-scene vs. out-of-scene generalization, object-centric vs. full-scene and background-only splits, plus a greedy feature-selection study and a CNN-based study on spatial neighborhoods (72 trained CNNs).

The claimed out-of-scene generalization of the regression models is a genuinely new capability for UE in GS, and the results (e.g., object-centric multi-scene correlations up to ~0.65–0.88 in Tables 13–14) support moderate transferability across scenes.

The greedy feature-removal analysis (Fig. 2) yields interesting insights (FoV counter dominance in full-scene UE, max-aggregation visibility with dropped opacity being key for object-centric UE, training-error features being least informative), which is valuable to the community beyond the specific method.

The paper is honest about negative or mixed findings, e.g., direction-dependent features hurting on TUM, linear regression sometimes beating gradient boosting, and failure to generalize to the outdoor scene 'torch'.
weaknesses: The baseline comparison is too narrow for the 'new state-of-the-art' claim: only FisherRF (plus a modified regression variant of it) is evaluated. Other UE-in-GS methods discussed in the paper — Aria et al. [1], Wilson et al. [39], Han & Dumery [6] — are not compared empirically. The large AUSE improvements (claimed 75–78 percentage points) partly reflect FisherRF performing poorly (even negative Pearson correlations on TUM), so the margin over a stronger comparison set is unknown.

The evaluation scope is limited to small, object-centric scenes (4 LF + 11 TUM scenes with a central object). It remains unclear how the method behaves on large-scale or unbounded scenes (e.g., Mip-NeRF 360-style data), where UE would arguably matter most for the robotics/medical applications cited.

The method requires holdout views with ground truth (rendered color/depth error targets) to train the regression model per scene. While the authors demonstrate cross-scene generalization, this supervised requirement and its practical implications (how many GT views, what camera coverage) are not critically discussed as a limitation relative to unsupervised UE methods.

Correlation numbers for rendering error on TUM are only moderate (~0.3 full-scene), and several trends are inconsistent across datasets (direction-dependent features help on LF but hurt on TUM), which weakens the generality of the framework's narrative. No statistical uncertainty (e.g., variance over repeated regression runs or seeds) is reported.

Presentation and reproducibility issues: numerous typos ('oppacity', 'Adressing', 'performe', 'Ituitively', 'peek'), the code release link is a placeholder (github.com/TBA), and the multi-column result tables are dense and hard to parse. Hyperparameters such as κ=8 and SH degree 4 are chosen empirically but without sensitivity analysis.

The key insight — that visibility/error statistics of Gaussians rendered into feature maps carry uncertainty information — is somewhat incremental in methodology; the main gains come from combining many hand-crafted features with standard gradient boosting, and the ablations show that no single component is decisively responsible for the improvements.

strengths: The proposed post-processing approach is practical: it does not interfere with GS training and requires only a few hold-out views to fit the uncertainty regression, which distinguishes it from methods that modify GS training itself (e.g., [1, 6]).

The paper provides an unusually extensive set of experiments: in-scene vs. out-of-scene generalization, full-scene vs. object-centric vs. background evaluation, direction-dependent vs. independent representations, greedy feature-selection ablations (Fig. 2), a CNN/spatial-context study, and detailed per-scene results in the appendix (Tabs. 5-14).

The claim of out-of-scene generalization of UE regression models is interesting and, to the authors' knowledge, novel; the results (e.g., Tab. 4) show moderate but consistent cross-scene transfer, which is a meaningful contribution for practical UE.

The proposed uncertainty feature maps consistently outperform both the standard FisherRF baseline and a strengthened regression-FisherRF variant across two datasets and both depth and rendering error targets, e.g., object-centric depth correlations up to ~0.85 (Tab. 3) versus 0.70-0.76 for regression-FisherRF.
The analysis of which features matter (FoV counter, max-aggregated visibility with dropped opacity) is insightful and connects results to the underlying geometry of the capture setups.
weaknesses: The experimental comparison is too narrow for a claimed 'new state-of-the-art': the only external baseline is FisherRF [11] (a 2023 arXiv preprint). Other relevant UE-for-GS methods such as Aira et al. [1], Wilson et al. [39], and Han & Dumery [6] are discussed in related work but not compared against, so the SOTA claim is weakly supported.

The method requires ground-truth images (and for depth UE, ground-truth depth) of hold-out views to train the regression model. This substantially limits the practical utility in the very applications (robotics, medicine) motivating the paper, and this limitation is not discussed honestly. The out-of-scene variant removes holdout needs only after an expensive multi-scene training phase.

Evaluation breadth is limited: only 4 LF scenes and 11 TUM scenes, all object-centric with circular camera trajectories and GT depth only for selected hold-out views. No standard large-scale benchmarks (e.g., Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks and Temples) are used, making generalization of the conclusions unclear.

The choice of Pearson correlation as the main metric, and the explicit rejection of R^2 due to 'potential shift in ranges' (Sec. 4), is only partially convincing; correlation alone can hide systematic biases in the predicted uncertainty magnitudes, and AUSE results are relegated to secondary status.

Novelty is moderate: the core idea (projecting training-view errors/visibility onto primitives and regressing rendered feature maps against true errors) is a natural combination of known components (GS rendering, von Mises-Fisher directionality, meta-regression ideas the authors have used in prior detection/segmentation work [4, 7, 15, 18, 28, 29]), and results show only modest gains over the strengthened regression-FisherRF control in several settings.

Some headline numbers are cherry-adjacent: the conclusion highlights improvements of 'up to 75.8/78.3 percent points' in AUSE, but these arise mostly from very poor FisherRF AUSE on TUM (0.742); on several scenes (e.g., torch) baselines match or exceed the method, and direction-dependent features are inconsistent across datasets.

Reproducibility is currently not ensured: code is stated as 'github.com/TBA', and many design choices (κ=8, SH degree 4, visibility thresholds 1/255 and 1e-3, gradient boosting hyperparameters) are given only tersely.

Writing quality needs polish: numerous typos ('oppacity', 'Adressing', 'performe', 'Ituitively', 'compleat', 'Person correlations') and some imprecise notation (Eq. 7/8 drop the normalization of the vMF density inconsistently described) distract from the technical content.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and practical: projecting training-view rendering errors and visibility onto Gaussian primitives, rendering these representations as uncertainty feature maps, and aggregating them via lightweight regression yields a purely post-processing UE method that does not interfere with GS training and requires only a few holdout views.

The empirical study is unusually thorough: in-scene and out-of-scene generalization, direction-dependent (von Mises-Fisher) vs. direction-independent representations, full-scene vs. object-centric evaluation, depth vs. rendering error, two regression model families, a greedy feature-selection study identifying the FoV counter and max-aggregated visibility as key features, and a CNN experiment on spatial context (Fig. 3).

The out-of-scene generalization of the regression models (Tabs. 4, 11-14) is an interesting and arguably novel capability, showing that the uncertainty feature maps capture partially scene-independent error patterns.

The authors are transparent about weaknesses: gradient boosting overfitting, direction-dependent features being detrimental on TUM, failure to generalize to the only outdoor scene (torch), and cases where linear regression or regression-FisherRF wins.

Evaluation on both depth error and rendering error, plus a fair attempt to strengthen the baseline (regression-FisherRF with 6 grouped FisherRF feature maps) so that the comparison isolates the quality of the proposed features rather than the regression machinery.
weaknesses: Baseline coverage is too narrow for the SOTA claims. The only comparison is against FisherRF [11] and a self-constructed 'regression-FisherRF' variant. Other GS UE methods cited in the related work (Wilson et al. [39], Aria et al. [1], the direction-dependent preprint [6]) are not empirically compared, so 'outperforming state-of-the-art methods' in the abstract is only substantiated against one baseline family. This is a material weakness for a paper whose main claim is empirical superiority.

The datasets are narrow: 4 LF scenes and 11 TUM scenes, all object-centric with camera trajectories circling a central object. No standard NVS/GS benchmarks (e.g., Mip-NeRF 360-style scenes), no real outdoor evaluation (the single outdoor scene, torch, is exactly where generalization fails), which limits evidence for applicability to robotics/medicine as motivated in the introduction.

The method depends on holdout views with ground truth (or near-GT rendered/depth errors) to fit the regression. For a new scene without such data, one must rely on regressors trained on other scenes, where correlations drop to moderate levels (e.g., full-scene depth correlation of ~0.15-0.4 on LF, occasionally negative in Tab. 11). This caveat deserves more prominent treatment than it receives.

The design of the 13 feature maps is largely heuristic (aggregation choices max/sum/mean, dropping opacity, FoV counting via view-cone binning, rescaled vMF with hand-picked κ=8 and SH degree 4). While the ablations justify the choices post hoc, the method reads as a bundle of empirical heuristics rather than a principled uncertainty model; no theoretical connection between the features and predictive variance/error is established.

Results are mixed in places and no statistical significance testing is reported: on LF scene *torch*, regression-FisherRF outperforms the method in AUSE; FisherRF (a negative-correlation method on TUM) is 'outperformed' partly because its correlations are near zero or negative; many out-of-scene cells are close to zero. Averages over a handful of scenes with single-run experiments make some claimed trends fragile.

Presentation has numerous errors that should be fixed: typos ('oppacity', 'Ituitively', 'performe', 'compleat', 'board plateau', 'peek'), a placeholder code URL (github.com/TBA) undermining the reproducibility claim at submission time, and confusing table layouts (e.g., Table 4's 'training' column for m-scene rows is hard to parse; the naming of 9a/9b/9c and 6a/6b/6c subsets requires cross-referencing the feature-selection section).

strengths: The proposed framework is technically sound and clearly motivated: it is a purely post-hoc method that requires no GS retraining, yet outperforms both post-hoc (FisherRF, BayesRays) and stochastic-radiance-field baselines (var3DGS, manifold) in AUSE and Pearson correlation for rendering and depth UE (Tabs. 1-3), with large margins in depth UE (e.g., Pearson 0.72 vs. 0.24 on LF).

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: experiments span four datasets, a scene/object/background separation study, an out-of-scene generalization study (Appendix C), a feature-combination/backward-selection analysis (Fig. 4, Tabs. 4-5), a spatial-interaction study with CNNs (Appendix E), and extensive qualitative comparisons (Figs. 3, 6-9).

The introduction of a regression-based FisherRF variant (Appendix A) strengthens fairness of comparison, since it isolates the contribution of the proposed primitive features from the meta-regression step, and PRIMU still outperforms it across all settings.

The demonstration that a single feature map (direction-dependent coverage with max aggregation and dropped opacity) suffices for active view selection, beating FisherRF and manifold under their own protocol (Tab. 6), is a practically useful and simple by-product that requires no holdout data or trained regressor.

The ablations are informative and honestly reported: e.g., the authors transparently show that direction-dependent features only marginally help for depth UE, that no reduced feature subset improves over the full 13 maps, and that out-of-scene generalization degrades in some depth settings (App. C).
weaknesses: The method amounts to handcrafted feature engineering plus a per-pixel meta-regressor; while effective, the conceptual novelty is moderate, and the choice of 13 features (aggregators, κ=8, SH degree 4) is largely empirical without a systematic justification or sensitivity analysis of these hyperparameters.

Uncertainty targets are rendering/depth error and the regressor requires ground-truth holdout views; this weakens the 'safety-critical deployment' motivation, since truly novel environments may not provide such supervision. Calibration of the produced uncertainties is not evaluated.

Absolute rendering-UE performance in the entire-scene setting remains modest (Pearson ~0.2-0.46), and improvements over the regression-based FisherRF baseline are sometimes small (e.g., AUSE 0.244 vs 0.282 on LF); statistical significance or variance over seeds/scenes is not reported, and the number of scenes is limited (4 LF scenes, 11 TUM scenes).

The AVS evaluation is narrow: it follows FisherRF's protocol with only two baselines, and the proposed selection criterion (coverage maximization) is conceptually close to Kopanas & Drettakis [15]'s observation-frequency approach, which is cited but not compared empirically.

Presentation issues reduce polish: repeated typos ('maniflod', 'Leaned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity', 'Gaoli et al.'), and rendering-quality claims for baselines (e.g., var3DGS PSNR 23.1 on LF) are reported without discussion of whether baseline numbers match original publications.

Computational cost of constructing the 13 feature maps, rendering them for each candidate view, and training the regressors is not reported, which matters for assessing practicality in robotics/AVS use cases.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem (post-hoc uncertainty estimation for Gaussian Splatting) with a genuinely post-processing approach that requires no GS retraining, which is attractive for real deployments.

The experimental evaluation is broad: four datasets (MipNeRF360, LLFF, LF, TUM), two error types (RGB and depth), standard UE metrics (AUSE, Pearson), plus an active view selection application that beats FisherRF and manifold in their own evaluation protocol (Tab. 6).

The paper is commendably transparent about the potentially unfair aspect of its comparison: it introduces a regression-based FisherRF variant (Appendix A, Tab. 3) that receives the same meta-regression treatment, and PRIMU still outperforms it across settings — this strengthens the claim that the primitive-level features themselves, not just the regression step, carry the benefit.

Thorough ablation and analysis: direction-dependent vs. independent features, foreground/background scene separation, step-wise backward feature selection (Fig. 4, Tabs. 4-5), out-of-scene generalization (Appendix C), and a spatial-interaction CNN study (Appendix E).
The active view selection result is notable because PRIMU-AVS needs no regression model or holdout data, outperforming baselines that explicitly estimate information gain.
weaknesses: Conceptual concern about what is being measured: the 'uncertainty features' are rendered projections of training-view errors and coverage, and the regressor is supervised with true errors on holdout views. To a substantial extent the method is a learned interpolation/extrapolation of training-view errors onto novel views, rather than an intrinsic uncertainty model. This makes it conceptually closer to an error-prediction heuristic than to uncertainty quantification as formulated by FisherRF, BayesRays, or stochastic GS methods, and raises questions about whether it can flag errors on views or scene regions unlike anything seen in training (the modest generalization correlations in Tab. 8, often 0.1-0.5, support this concern).

Absolute performance outside object-centric settings is weak: entire-scene rendering-UE Pearson correlations are only ~0.2-0.46 and AUSE ~0.22-0.34 (Tabs. 1, 3), yet the abstract claims 'strong correlations with true errors.' The headline gains are concentrated on object-centric depth UE, where coverage/FoV features trivially help; the paper should temper its claims.

Novelty is moderate: the core idea is a set of 13 handcrafted, heuristic feature maps (FoV counts, aggregated opacity-weighted coverage and error projections, plus a von Mises-Fisher direction weighting). The design space is explored empirically rather than motivated from first principles, and no feature set consistently dominates, suggesting the contribution is more a well-engineered recipe than a principled advance.

Fairness of the main comparisons (Tabs. 1-2): PRIMU is trained per scene with ground-truth errors from holdout views, while FisherRF, var3DGS, and manifold use no ground truth at all. The regression-based FisherRF control appears only in the scene-separation study, not in the headline tables, leaving the main tables somewhat apples-to-oranges.
No statement about code release; given the many implementation choices (13 feature maps, κ=8, degree-4 SH, aggregation variants, thresholds α≥1/255, T≥1e-3), reproducibility without code is doubtful.

Presentation issues that should have been caught: repeated typos ('maniflod', 'Leaned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity', 'which are aggregate', 'rendeing'), and inconsistent figures (Fig. 7 caption says 'ℓ1 rendering error' for depth UE). These are minor but reflect limited polish.

strengths: The proposed method is well-motivated and technically sound: projecting training-view errors and coverage statistics onto Gaussian primitives and rendering them as uncertainty feature maps is an elegant, interpretable post-hoc formulation that requires no GS retraining and does not degrade rendering quality (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS identical to vanilla GS in Tables 1-2).

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: UE experiments on four datasets (MipNeRF360, LLFF, LF, TUM), a scene-separation study with a carefully constructed regression-based FisherRF baseline (Appendix A), out-of-scene generalization experiments (Appendix C, Table 8), a feature-map combination/ablation study (Tables 4-5, Fig. 4), and a supplementary CNN study on spatial interaction (Appendix E).

Results support the main claims: PRIMU consistently outperforms FisherRF, var3DGS, and manifold on rendering UE (Table 1) and depth UE (Table 2, e.g., AUSE 0.115 vs. 0.305 for FisherRF on LF depth), with particularly strong object-centric performance (AUSE < 0.1, correlations > 0.8 with a single hold-out view, Table 3).

The AVS application is a nice, practically useful demonstration: using the coverage feature map directly (without a regressor or hold-out data) outperforms FisherRF and manifold on MipNeRF360 AVS (Table 6), matching the stated goal of data-efficient view selection.

The paper is clearly written, the method is fully specified (Eqs. 1-8, hyperparameters such as κ=8 and SH degree 4), and the ablations provide genuine insight into which feature maps matter (FoV counter, max-aggregated opacity-free coverage).
weaknesses: The core idea is conceptually simple — accumulating per-pixel training errors and visibility onto primitives — and the main performance gain arguably comes from the learned meta-regression on top of 13 handcrafted features rather than from a deep technical contribution. Reviewers may view this as incremental relative to FisherRF-style post-hoc uncertainty plus regression.

The method requires at least one hold-out view with ground truth (rendering or depth error) to train the regressor. This weakens the 'safety-critical deployment' motivation, since such ground truth is precisely what is often unavailable in robotics/medical settings. The cross-scene generalization results (Appendix C) partially mitigate this, but rendering-UE correlations degrade substantially (e.g., ~0.2-0.3 in Table 8 for LF).

Absolute uncertainty quality for rendering error on entire scenes is modest: best Pearson correlations are only ~0.35-0.46 (Tables 1, 3, 4), and the headline SOTA claim rests on comparisons where baseline correlations are near zero or negative (e.g., FisherRF -0.13 on LF, -0.088 on LLFF). Such extreme baseline failures raise questions about baseline tuning/evaluation protocol; at minimum, the gap in absolute terms is smaller than the relative numbers suggest.

The choice of 13 feature maps appears somewhat ad hoc; the ablation (Tables 4-5) shows reduced sets retain nearly all performance but no reduced configuration consistently improves results, leaving the practical benefit of the extra maps unclear.

Evaluation is limited to AUSE and Pearson correlation; no calibration analysis (e.g., calibration curves or NLL-style metrics) is provided, which is relevant for the safety-critical use cases invoked in the introduction.
No explicit statement about code release, which limits reproducibility of the multi-component pipeline (feature map extraction, vMF-based direction-dependent features, regression setup).

Minor presentation issues: typos ('maniflod', 'Leaned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity', 'rendeing' in Appendix A), and FisherRF on LLFF reporting AUSE 0.988 (near-random) deserves more discussion than it receives.
